catalog_quote: The syllable structure of Nyah Kur words is rendered extremely complex by extensive Thai loans, resulting in such word shapes as CCCVCV́VC (/phyəyáam/ 'to try') and CV́CCVCCV́C (/sókkəprók/ 'dirty'). If we confine ourselves to native Nyah Kur words, they may be either 1) monosyllabic of shape C(C)(C)(C)(C){V́C / V́V(C)} (as illustrated in 1.3.1.1.), implying that a final /C/ is obligatory after short vowels but optional after long vowels and diphthongs; or 2) disyllabic, consisting of an unstressed presyllable of shape /CV-/, where /V/ is always /ə/, plus a stressed syllable having one of the shapes represented in 1) above.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Native Nyah Kur words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables; in disyllables the initial presyllable /Cə-/ is unstressed and the final (main) syllable carries the stress, i.e. word stress is fixed on the final syllable. Confirmed independently by Bunphan 1982 (Chulalongkorn MA, p.8, Thai): 'ส่วนพยางค์รองประกอบด้วยพยัญชนะเดี่ยวและสระลดรูป /ə/ ทั้งนี้เนื่องจากพยางค์รองเป็นพยางค์ที่ไม่ได้รับการลงเสียงหนัก (unstressed syllable) ฉะนั้นในการบันทึกลักษณะน้ำเสียงจะใส่เครื่องหมายแสดงลักษณะน้ำเสียงเฉพาะพยางค์หลักเท่านั้น' [the minor syllable consists of a single consonant and the reduced vowel /ə/; since the minor syllable is a syllable that does not receive stress (unstressed syllable), register is marked only on the major syllable], file.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said. Polysyllabic Thai loans (e.g. /sókkəprók/) carry Huffman's acute mark on each full syllable, but he does not discuss secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Thai loanwords produce longer word shapes with more than one full syllable and may retain Thai tones (pp.51-52, 56); the fixed-final statement is made for native vocabulary. Nyah Kur is a register (clear vs breathy) language; pitch differences accompany register but are described as non-contrastive.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word in citation form (elicited 900-word vocabulary from one speaker, Ban Wang Ai Pho, Amphoe Bamnet Narong, Chaiyaphum, 1970-71). Stress is described via word/syllable structure (presyllable vs main syllable), not phrase prosody.
new_statements.identity_note: Huffman 1990 describes Nyah Kur of Ban Wang Ai Pho, Amphoe Bamnet Narong, Chaiyaphum Province (the central/southern dialect group in L-Thongkum's classification); Bunphan 1982 draws on L-Thongkum's dictionary data (Chaiyaphum/Nakhon Ratchasima southern group). Both fall under glottocode nyah1250 (language-level); the northern Phetchabun dialect is not covered by the quoted statement.

sources.note: p.56 sec. 1.3.3 (Nyah Kur of Ban Wang Ai Pho, Chaiyaphum): native words are either monosyllables or disyllables consisting of an unstressed presyllable /Cə-/ plus a stressed (main, final) syllable; Thai loans add more complex shapes. Also notes register (clear vs breathy) with non-contrastive pitch, and Thai loans retaining tones (pp.51-52).
